questions.question: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair? A: the weight of the book and the upward force of the table on the book; B: the weight of the book and the downward force of the book on the table; C: the upward force of the table on the book and the weight of the table; D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table.
questions.answer: D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table
steps: A Newton's third law pair consists of two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, that act on two different bodies and arise from the same interaction.
The table pushes up on the book (a contact force) and the book pushes down on the table (a contact force): same type, equal and opposite, on different bodies. This is D.
A is wrong: both forces act on the book and they balance each other, which is the first law, not the third. They are also different types of force.
B is wrong because the weight is a gravitational force, so its third-law partner is the book's pull on the Earth. C involves the table's weight, which is not part of the same interaction.

questions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg tows a trailer of mass 350 kg along a straight horizontal road. The car and trailer accelerate at 1.4 m s^-2. The total resistive force acting on the trailer is 120 N. What is the tension in the tow bar? A: 370 N; B: 490 N; C: 610 N; D: 2170 N.
steps: Consider only the trailer. The tension T in the tow bar acts forwards and the resistive force of 120 N acts backwards.
Newton's second law: T - 120 = 350 x 1.4 = 490, so T = 490 + 120 = 610 N (C).
A subtracts the resistive force instead of adding it. B forgets the resistive force.
D uses the total mass of the car and trailer (1550 kg x 1.4 = 2170 N), which gives the resultant force on the whole system, not the tension in the tow bar.

questions.question: A crane lifts a container of mass 850 kg using a vertical cable. At one instant the tension in the cable is 9.6 kN. Calculate the acceleration of the container at this instant.
questions.answer: Acceleration = 1.5 m s^-2 upwards
steps: Weight of container = m g = 850 x 9.81 = 8338.5 N.
Resultant force upwards = T - mg = 9600 - 8338.5 = 1261.5 N.
a = resultant force / mass = 1261.5 / 850 = 1.48 m s^-2 = 1.5 m s^-2 upwards.

questions.question: State Newton's third law of motion and explain why the two forces in a third-law pair do not cancel each other out.
questions.answer: If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A; the forces act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel.
steps: When body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force on A (the two forces form an interaction pair)
The two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The forces act on different bodies, and forces cancel only if they act on the same body, so they cannot cancel
accept: The two forces are of the same type (for example both gravitational or both contact forces)
The two forces exist at the same time and one cannot exist without the other
Example: the Earth pulls on a book and the book pulls on the Earth with equal and opposite forces
A resultant is found only by adding forces that act on one body

questions.question: A trolley of mass 0.80 kg is on a horizontal track and is connected by a light string, passing over a frictionless pulley, to a hanging mass of 0.20 kg. The trolley is released. Friction on the trolley is negligible. Calculate the acceleration of the trolley and the tension in the string.
questions.answer: Acceleration = 2.0 m s^-2; tension = 1.6 N
steps: Hanging mass: m g - T = m a, so 0.20 x 9.81 - T = 0.20 a.
Trolley: the only horizontal force is the tension, so T = 0.80 a.
T = 0.80 x 1.962 = 1.57 N = 1.6 N (less than the weight of the hanging mass, 1.96 N, as it accelerates downwards).

questions.question: A lift of total mass 1500 kg is raised by a single vertical cable. The lift moves upwards at a constant speed of 2.0 m s^-1. Calculate the tension in the cable.
questions.answer: Tension = 1.47 x 10^4 N
steps: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the resultant force is zero (Newton's first law).

questions.question: A lift of total mass 1500 kg is raised by a single vertical cable. The lift accelerates upwards at 1.2 m s^-2. Calculate the tension in the cable.
questions.answer: Tension = 1.65 x 10^4 N
steps: Resultant upward force = T - m g = m a.

questions.question: A lift of total mass 1500 kg is raised by a single vertical cable. A passenger of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing machine in the lift while the lift accelerates upwards at 1.2 m s^-2. Calculate the force exerted by the machine on the passenger and compare it with the passenger's weight.
questions.answer: Force = 771 N, which is greater than the weight of 687 N
steps: Resultant upward force on the passenger = R - m g = m a.
The passenger's weight is 70 x 9.81 = 686.7 N = 687 N, so the force from the machine is greater than the weight (the reading is higher).

questions.question: A lift of total mass 1500 kg is raised by a single vertical cable. The cable can safely support a maximum tension of 24 kN. Determine the maximum upward acceleration of the lift and suggest why lifts are designed to accelerate much more slowly than this.
questions.answer: Maximum acceleration = 6.19 m s^-2. A lift accelerating this fast would make passengers feel about 1.6 times heavier, which is uncomfortable and unsafe, and it would leave no safety margin on the cable.
steps: At the maximum tension, T - m g = m a.
At this acceleration the force on a passenger from the floor is m (g + a), about 1.6 times the passenger's weight, which is uncomfortable and could injure people.
Operating with the cable at its maximum tension would leave no safety margin, so real lifts accelerate far more slowly.
accept: Passengers could lose their balance or fall over if the lift starts or stops so abruptly
Large accelerations would put the cable, motor and lift structure under extra stress and wear
The cable needs a safety margin to allow for extra load or snatching of the cable

questions.question: A box of mass m is at rest on a rough slope that is inclined at an angle theta to the horizontal. What is the frictional force acting on the box? A: mg cos(theta); B: mg sin(theta); C: mg tan(theta); D: mg.
questions.answer: B: mg sin(theta)
steps: The box is in equilibrium, so the resultant force on it is zero.
Along the slope, the component of the weight down the slope is mg sin(theta). The only other force along the slope is friction, acting up the slope.
So the frictional force = mg sin(theta), which is B.
mg cos(theta) is the component of the weight perpendicular to the slope, which is balanced by the normal reaction force. C and D do not correspond to any component of the weight along the slope.

questions.question: A crate of mass 12 kg slides down a rough slope that is inclined at 25 degrees to the horizontal. The crate accelerates down the slope at 1.9 m s^-2. What is the frictional force acting on the crate? A: 27 N; B: 50 N; C: 73 N; D: 84 N.
questions.answer: A: 27 N
steps: Take down the slope as positive. Newton's second law along the slope: m g sin(25) - F = m a.
B ignores the acceleration, C adds m a instead of subtracting it, and D uses cos 25 instead of sin 25.

questions.question: A block of mass 4.0 kg rests on a rough slope inclined at 20 degrees to the horizontal. The block is in equilibrium. Calculate the frictional force and the normal reaction force acting on the block.
questions.answer: Frictional force = 13 N (up the slope); normal reaction = 37 N
steps: The block is in equilibrium, so the forces balance both along and perpendicular to the slope.
Along the slope: friction = component of weight down the slope = m g sin 20 = 4.0 x 9.81 x sin 20 = 13.42 N = 13 N.
Perpendicular to the slope: normal reaction = m g cos 20 = 4.0 x 9.81 x cos 20 = 36.87 N = 37 N.

questions.question: Explain why the braking distance of a car is longer on a wet road than on a dry road when the car brakes from the same initial speed.
questions.answer: Less friction on a wet road gives a smaller maximum braking force and deceleration, so the braking distance s = u^2 / (2a) is longer.
steps: The braking force on the car is the frictional force between the tyres and the road
Water reduces the maximum friction, so the braking force is smaller and the deceleration (a = F / m) is smaller
For the same initial speed s = u^2 / (2a), so a smaller deceleration gives a longer braking distance
accept: The tyres may skid or aquaplane on a layer of water, reducing friction further
The same kinetic energy must be removed by work done against friction (W = F s), so a smaller force needs a longer distance
The thinking distance is unchanged, but the total stopping distance is longer

questions.question: A car of mass 650 kg rolls down a straight hill inclined at 8.0 degrees to the horizontal at a constant speed with the engine off. Determine the total resistive force acting on the car.
questions.answer: Resistive force = 8.9 x 10^2 N, directed up the slope
steps: Constant speed means no acceleration, so the resultant force along the slope is zero (Newton's first law).
The component of the weight down the slope is m g sin 8.0 = 650 x 9.81 x sin 8.0 = 887.4 N.
The resistive force (air resistance and friction) acts up the slope and equals this: 8.9 x 10^2 N.

questions.question: A crate of mass 25 kg is pulled up a rough slope, inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal, by a rope parallel to the slope. Calculate the component of the weight of the crate parallel to the slope.
questions.answer: Component = 123 N
steps: Component parallel to the slope = m g sin 30.

questions.question: A crate of mass 25 kg is pulled up a rough slope, inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal, by a rope parallel to the slope. The crate moves up the slope at constant speed when the tension in the rope is 190 N. Calculate the frictional force acting on the crate.
questions.answer: Frictional force = 67.4 N (down the slope)
steps: Constant speed: the forces along the slope balance, so tension = weight component + friction.
Friction = 190 - 122.6 = 67.4 N, acting down the slope.

questions.question: A crate of mass 25 kg is pulled up a rough slope, inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal, by a rope parallel to the slope. The crate is moving up the slope at 2.4 m s^-1 when the rope breaks. Assume the frictional force stays at 67.4 N. Calculate the deceleration of the crate and the distance it moves up the slope before stopping.
questions.answer: Deceleration = 7.6 m s^-2; distance = 0.379 m
steps: After the rope breaks, both the weight component (122.6 N) and the friction (67.4 N) act down the slope
Resultant force = 122.6 + 67.4 = 190 N
a = 190 / 25 = 7.6 m s^-2 (a deceleration, down the slope)

questions.question: A crate of mass 25 kg is pulled up a rough slope, inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal, by a rope parallel to the slope. The crate has come to rest on the slope and the rope is no longer attached. The frictional force the slope can exert on the crate is at most 67.4 N, and it has this value while the crate slides. Deduce what happens next and calculate the magnitude of the initial acceleration.
questions.answer: The crate slides back down the slope because the weight component (123 N) is greater than the maximum friction (67.4 N); initial acceleration = 2.21 m s^-2.
steps: Resultant force down the slope = 122.6 - 67.4 = 55.2 N (friction now acts up the slope).
a = 55.2 / 25 = 2.21 m s^-2 down the slope.
The weight component (122.6 N) is greater than the maximum friction (67.4 N), so the forces cannot balance and the crate slides back down the slope.
accept: Friction can only balance the weight component if the weight component is no more than the maximum friction
The direction of the friction reverses when the crate changes from moving up to moving down
The crate would remain at rest only if the maximum friction were at least 122.6 N

questions.question: Two trolleys collide on a horizontal track and friction is negligible. The collision is inelastic. Which statement about the total momentum and the total kinetic energy of the trolleys is correct? A: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy decreases; B: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy is conserved; C: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy is conserved; D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases.
questions.answer: D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases
steps: Momentum is conserved in every collision when no external resultant force acts. Friction is negligible, so the total momentum is conserved.
In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (thermal energy, sound, deformation), so the total kinetic energy decreases.
This is D. A and C wrongly say momentum decreases; B describes an elastic collision.

questions.question: A trolley of mass 0.40 kg moving at 1.5 m s^-1 collides with a stationary trolley of mass 0.60 kg. The trolleys stick together and move off with a common velocity. What is the speed of the trolleys after the collision? A: 0.60 m s^-1; B: 0.75 m s^-1; C: 1.0 m s^-1; D: 1.5 m s^-1.
steps: Momentum before = 0.40 x 1.5 + 0.60 x 0 = 0.60 kg m s^-1.
Momentum after = (0.40 + 0.60) v = 1.00 v. Conservation of momentum gives v = 0.60 m s^-1 (A).
B is the average of 1.5 and 0. C divides by 0.60 kg only and D divides by 0.40 kg only, instead of using the total mass.

questions.question: A gun of mass 2.4 kg is free to move. It fires a bullet of mass 15 g at a speed of 380 m s^-1. The gun and bullet are initially at rest. Calculate the recoil speed of the gun.
questions.answer: Recoil speed = 2.4 m s^-1
steps: The total momentum before firing is zero, so after firing the momenta are equal and opposite: M V = m v.
Mass of bullet = 15 g = 0.015 kg.
V = m v / M = 0.015 x 380 / 2.4 = 2.375 m s^-1 = 2.4 m s^-1, in the opposite direction to the bullet.

questions.question: A car has a crumple zone at the front. Explain, using the idea of impulse, how this reduces the force on the occupants in a collision.
questions.answer: The crumple zone increases the stopping time for the same change of momentum, so the average force (change of momentum / time) on the occupants is smaller.
steps: The change of momentum of the occupants is fixed by their mass and the speed before the collision
The crumple zone collapses progressively, so the time taken to stop is increased
Force = change of momentum / time, so a longer time gives a smaller average force on the occupants (less injury)
accept: The crumple zone deforms and absorbs kinetic energy, so less energy is transferred to the occupants
Seat belts and airbags work in the same way by increasing the stopping time
The impulse F t is constant, so F is inversely proportional to t

questions.question: A tennis ball of mass 0.057 kg hits a vertical wall horizontally at 18 m s^-1 and rebounds along the same line at 12 m s^-1. The ball is in contact with the wall for 8.0 ms. Calculate the average force exerted by the wall on the ball.
questions.answer: Average force = 2.1 x 10^2 N, directed away from the wall
steps: Take the initial direction of the ball as positive: initial velocity = +18 m s^-1, final velocity = -12 m s^-1.
Change in momentum = m (v - u) = 0.057 x (-12 - 18) = -1.71 kg m s^-1.
Force = change in momentum / time = 1.71 / 0.0080 = 214 N.
Average force = 2.1 x 10^2 N, directed away from the wall (opposite to the initial velocity).

questions.question: Glider A, of mass 0.35 kg, moves along a horizontal air track at 0.80 m s^-1 towards glider B, of mass 0.15 kg, which is stationary. After the collision glider A continues in the same direction at 0.40 m s^-1. State the principle of conservation of linear momentum.
questions.answer: The total momentum of a system before an interaction equals the total momentum after it, provided no external resultant force acts.
steps: The total momentum of a system of interacting bodies before a collision equals the total momentum after it (in a given direction)
provided no external resultant force acts on the system (a closed or isolated system)
accept: Momentum is conserved in elastic and in inelastic collisions
The momentum gained by one body equals the momentum lost by the other
Total momentum is conserved separately in each of two perpendicular directions

questions.question: Glider A, of mass 0.35 kg, moves along a horizontal air track at 0.80 m s^-1 towards glider B, of mass 0.15 kg, which is stationary. After the collision glider A continues in the same direction at 0.40 m s^-1. Calculate the velocity of glider B after the collision.
questions.answer: Velocity of B = 0.93 m s^-1 in the original direction of A
steps: Momentum before = 0.35 x 0.80 + 0.15 x 0 = 0.280 kg m s^-1.

questions.question: Glider A, of mass 0.35 kg, moves along a horizontal air track at 0.80 m s^-1 towards glider B, of mass 0.15 kg, which is stationary. After the collision glider A continues in the same direction at 0.40 m s^-1. Glider B moves off at 0.93 m s^-1. Deduce whether the collision is elastic, and suggest where any kinetic energy that is lost has gone.
questions.answer: Not elastic: kinetic energy before = 0.112 J, after = 0.093 J, so about 0.019 J is lost (to thermal energy and sound, and any deformation).
steps: Kinetic energy before = 0.5 x 0.35 x 0.80^2 = 0.112 J.
Kinetic energy is not conserved (it falls by about 0.019 J), so the collision is inelastic.
The lost energy is transferred to thermal energy and sound (and to deformation of the gliders' bumpers).
accept: Energy transferred as sound when the gliders collide
Thermal energy in the gliders and the surrounding air
Energy used to deform or compress the bumpers or springs on the gliders

questions.question: A uniform beam of weight 120 N is pivoted at its centre. A load of 250 N hangs 1.2 m to the left of the pivot. At what distance to the right of the pivot must a load of 200 N hang for the beam to balance horizontally? A: 0.67 m; B: 0.96 m; C: 1.2 m; D: 1.5 m.
steps: The weight of the uniform beam acts at its centre, which is at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
For balance, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: 200 x d = 250 x 1.2 = 300 N m.
A divides the moment by the total of the loads, B turns the ratio upside down, and C assumes the two loads must be the same distance from the pivot.

questions.question: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.36 m by applying a force of 8.5 N to each side of the wheel. The forces are tangential, equal and opposite, and form a couple. What is the torque of the couple? A: 1.5 N m; B: 3.1 N m; C: 6.1 N m; D: 17 N m.
questions.answer: B: 3.1 N m
steps: The torque of a couple = one of the forces x the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces.
The forces act at opposite ends of a diameter, so the distance between them is 0.36 m.
A uses the radius (0.18 m), C counts both forces and the full diameter, and D adds the forces and ignores the distance.

questions.question: State the two conditions that must be satisfied for a rigid body acted on by coplanar forces to be in equilibrium.
questions.answer: The resultant force on the body is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.
steps: The resultant (vector sum of the) force on the body is zero
The sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point (the resultant moment is zero)
accept: The forces form a closed polygon (a closed triangle for three forces) when drawn head to tail
The components of the forces resolved in each of two perpendicular directions sum to zero
There is no resultant turning effect about any axis

questions.question: A uniform horizontal beam AB, of length 6.0 m and weight 450 N, rests on two vertical supports. One support is at end A and the other is at point C, which is 1.5 m from end B. Calculate the force exerted by each support on the beam.
questions.answer: Force at A = 150 N; force at C = 300 N (both upwards)
steps: The weight of the beam acts at its centre, 3.0 m from A. C is 6.0 - 1.5 = 4.5 m from A, so the weight is 1.5 m from C.
Take moments about C (this removes the unknown force at C): RA x 4.5 = 450 x 1.5.
Vertical equilibrium: RA + RC = 450, so RC = 450 - 150 = 300 N.

questions.question: A tall bus with a high centre of gravity is parked on a road that slopes sideways. Explain why the bus is more likely to topple over than a low sports car on the same road.
questions.answer: The vehicle topples once the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside the wheels; a high centre of gravity reaches this at a smaller tilt.
steps: The weight acts vertically downwards through the centre of gravity
If the vertical line through the centre of gravity falls outside the base (the downhill wheels), the weight has a resultant moment about those wheels that turns the vehicle over
A higher centre of gravity moves this line outside the base at a smaller angle of tilt, so the bus topples more easily
accept: A low centre of gravity means the vehicle must tilt much further before the line of the weight passes outside the base
A wider wheelbase (larger base) makes a vehicle more stable
Passengers on an upper deck or luggage on the roof raise the centre of gravity and make toppling more likely
Inside the base the weight gives a restoring moment about the downhill wheels

questions.question: A lamp of mass 12 kg hangs at rest from two light cables. The cables are attached to a ceiling at the same height and each makes an angle of 35 degrees with the horizontal. Calculate the tension in each cable.
questions.answer: Tension in each cable = 103 N
steps: The lamp is in equilibrium, so the resultant force is zero. By symmetry the tension T is the same in both cables.
Vertical components balance the weight: 2 T sin 35 = m g = 12 x 9.81 = 117.7 N.
The horizontal components of the two tensions are equal and opposite, so they cancel. T = 103 N.

questions.question: A uniform diving board AB, of length 3.0 m and mass 28 kg, rests horizontally. It is held down at end A by a clamp and rests on a pivot support at P, where AP = 0.80 m. Both supports exert vertical forces on the board. A diver of mass 65 kg stands at the free end B. Calculate the moment of the diver's weight about P.
questions.answer: Moment = 1.40 x 10^3 N m
steps: Distance PB = 3.0 - 0.80 = 2.2 m.
Moment = weight x perpendicular distance = 65 x 9.81 x 2.2 = 1402.8 N m = 1.40 x 10^3 N m.

questions.question: A uniform diving board AB, of length 3.0 m and mass 28 kg, rests horizontally. It is held down at end A by a clamp and rests on a pivot support at P, where AP = 0.80 m. Both supports exert vertical forces on the board. A diver of mass 65 kg stands at the free end B. The moment of the diver's weight about P is 1.40 x 10^3 N m. Calculate the force exerted by the clamp at A on the board.
questions.answer: Force at A = 1.99 x 10^3 N, downwards
steps: The weight of the uniform board acts at its centre, 1.5 m from A, which is 1.5 - 0.80 = 0.70 m from P on the same side as B.
Moment of the board's weight about P = 28 x 9.81 x 0.70 = 192.3 N m.
Take moments about P: FA x 0.80 = 1.40 x 10^3 + 192.3 = 1592 N m.

questions.question: A uniform diving board AB, of length 3.0 m and mass 28 kg, rests horizontally. It is held down at end A by a clamp and rests on a pivot support at P, where AP = 0.80 m. Both supports exert vertical forces on the board. A diver of mass 65 kg stands at the free end B. Calculate the force exerted on the board by the support at P.
questions.answer: Force at P = 2.91 x 10^3 N, upwards
steps: NP = 2906 N = 2.91 x 10^3 N upwards.
Check: vertical forces balance, NP = FA + weight of board + weight of diver = 1994 + 275 + 638 = 2906 N.

questions.question: A uniform diving board AB, of length 3.0 m and mass 28 kg, rests horizontally. It is held down at end A by a clamp and rests on a pivot support at P, where AP = 0.80 m. Both supports exert vertical forces on the board. A diver of mass 65 kg stands at the free end B. State the direction of the force exerted on the board by the clamp at A and explain your answer.
questions.answer: Downwards: the weights on the B side of P turn the board one way about P, so the clamp on the other side must push down to balance the turning effect.
steps: The weights of the diver and the board act on the B side of P and give a resultant moment about P that tends to lower B (and raise A)
For zero resultant moment, A (on the other side of P) must exert an equal moment in the opposite sense, which needs a downward force at A
accept: The board tends to rotate about P and lift end A, so the clamp must hold A down
Taking moments about P gives a positive (downward) value for the force at A
If A simply rested on a support, the board would tip with A rising
